nodes.label: Ozone Layer
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ozone (O3) at higher atmospheric levels shields Earth's surface from ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which causes skin cancer. Formed when UV radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms that combine with O2 to form O3. Ozone levels began dropping sharply in the 1980s due to synthetic chemicals like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). Though O3 is essential in the upper atmosphere, it is a deadly poison at ground level.

nodes.label: Ozone Depletion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The decrease in ozone concentration in the atmosphere, linked to synthetic chemicals especially CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. In 1987, UNEP (United Nations Environment Programme) forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels. It is now mandatory worldwide to manufacture CFC-free refrigerators. The ozone hole over Antarctica has been a major environmental concern.

nodes.label: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Synthetic chemicals that deplete the ozone layer. Used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. Their production was frozen at 1986 levels through a UNEP agreement in 1987. CFC-free refrigerators are now mandatory worldwide. CFCs are extremely stable in the lower atmosphere but break down in the stratosphere, releasing chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules.

nodes.label: Ultraviolet Radiation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: High-energy radiation from the Sun that is highly damaging to organisms. Known to cause skin cancer in humans. The ozone layer in the upper atmosphere shields Earth's surface from most UV radiation. UV radiation itself is responsible for creating ozone by splitting O2 molecules. Depletion of the ozone layer increases UV exposure at Earth's surface.

nodes.label: Ganga Action Plan
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Multi-crore project launched in 1985 to clean the Ganga, whose water quality had deteriorated severely. Coliform bacteria (found in human intestines) in water indicates contamination by disease-causing microorganisms. Despite the project, coliform levels remain high at many points along the river, from Gangotri to Diamond Harbour. Water quality can be checked using pH with universal indicator.

nodes.label: Chipko Andolan
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Grassroots 'Hug the Trees' movement originating from Reni village in Garhwal (Himalayas) in the early 1970s. Women villagers clasped tree trunks to prevent a logging contractor from felling trees when men were absent. Highlighted the conflict between industrial exploitation and community-based sustainable use. Communities traditionally lop branches and pluck leaves (allowing regrowth) rather than felling entire trees. Quickly spread across communities and forced government to rethink forest use priorities.

nodes.label: People's Participation in Forest Management
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Example: In 1972, West Bengal Forest Department's Arabari forest range (Midnapore district). A.K. Banerjee involved villagers in protecting 1,272 hectares of degraded sal forest. Villagers given employment in silviculture and harvesting, 25% of final harvest, and allowed fuelwood/fodder collection. By 1983, the previously worthless forest was valued at Rs 12.5 crores. Shows that participatory management is more effective than surveillance and policing.

nodes.label: Biodiversity Conservation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forests are 'biodiversity hotspots'. Biodiversity measured by number of species and range of life forms (bacteria, fungi, ferns, flowering plants, nematodes, insects, birds, reptiles). Loss of diversity leads to loss of ecological stability. Conservation must balance needs of local communities, industry, government, and environmentalists. Monoculture plantations (pine, teak, eucalyptus) destroy local biodiversity and fail to meet varied local needs.

nodes.label: Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: India was among the first countries to initiate national-level reproductive health programmes. Family planning programmes started in 1951, later expanded as RCH programmes. Focus areas: creating awareness about reproduction-related aspects, sex education in schools, providing medical facilities for pregnancy, delivery, STIs, contraception, infertility, and post-natal care. WHO defines reproductive health as total well-being in all aspects of reproduction - physical, emotional, behavioural, and social.

nodes.label: Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs/STIs)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Infections transmitted through sexual intercourse, also called STIs or VD or RTI. Common STIs: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B, and HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis-B and HIV can also spread through shared needles, blood transfusion, or mother-to-foetus. Hepatitis-B, genital herpes, and HIV infections are NOT completely curable. Complications include PID, abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility, or reproductive tract cancer. Highest incidence in 15-24 age group.

nodes.label: Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Techniques to help infertile couples have children. IVF (In Vitro Fertilisation/Test Tube Baby): ova and sperms collected, zygote formed in lab, then transferred - ZIFT (Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer, up to 8 blastomeres) or IUT (Intra Uterine Transfer, more than 8 blastomeres). GIFT (Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer): donor ovum transferred to fallopian tube of female who cannot produce ova. ICSI (Intra Cytoplasmic Sperm Injection): sperm directly injected into ovum in lab. AI (Artificial Insemination)/IUI: semen introduced into vagina or uterus.

nodes.label: DNA Replication (Semiconservative)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Proposed by Watson and Crick: each strand serves as template for new complementary strand. Proved semiconservative by Meselson and Stahl (1958) using N-15 heavy isotope in E. coli and CsCl density gradient centrifugation. After one generation: hybrid density DNA. After two: equal hybrid and light DNA. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase catalyses in 5'->3' direction only. At replication fork: one strand continuous synthesis, other discontinuous (Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase). Rate: ~2000 bp/sec in E. coli. Origin of replication required; occurs in S-phase of cell cycle.

nodes.label: DNA Fingerprinting
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Technique developed by Alec Jeffreys using Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR), a type of mini-satellite DNA. 99.9% of human DNA is identical; the 0.1% difference (mainly in repetitive/satellite DNA) creates unique patterns. Steps: DNA isolation, restriction enzyme digestion, electrophoresis separation, Southern blot transfer to membrane, hybridisation with labelled VNTR probe, autoradiography detection. Same pattern from all tissues of an individual. Identical only in monozygotic twins. Applications: forensic science, paternity testing, population genetics. PCR has increased sensitivity (single cell sufficient).

nodes.label: Miller-Urey Experiment
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In 1953, S.L. Miller (American scientist) recreated early earth conditions in the laboratory. He created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3, and water vapour at 800 degrees C. Result: formation of amino acids. Similar experiments by others produced sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments, and fats. Analysis of meteorite content revealed similar compounds. This provided experimental evidence for chemical evolution (first part of the origin of life story).

nodes.label: Brief Account of Evolution on Geological Time Scale
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: First cellular forms: ~2000 mya. Invertebrates active by 500 mya. Jawless fish: ~350 mya. Plants invaded land before animals. Fish with stout fins moved on land ~350 mya. Coelacanth (lobefin) found in South Africa (1938), thought extinct. Amphibians evolved from lobefins; reptiles from amphibians. Dinosaurs dominated for ~200 million years, including Tyrannosaurus rex (20 feet tall). Dinosaurs disappeared ~65 mya. First mammals were shrew-like. Australian marsupials survived due to continental drift and lack of competition. Marine mammals: whales, dolphins, seals.

nodes.label: Acquired Immunity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Pathogen-specific immunity characterized by memory. Primary response (first encounter, low intensity) and secondary/anamnestic response (subsequent encounter, highly intensified). Two types: (1) Humoral immune response - B-lymphocytes produce antibodies (IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG); (2) Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) - mediated by T-lymphocytes, responsible for graft rejection. T-cells help B-cells produce antibodies.

nodes.label: Antibodies (Immunoglobulins)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Proteins produced by B-lymphocytes in response to pathogens. Each antibody has four peptide chains: two light chains and two heavy chains (represented as H2L2). Types include IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG. Found in blood as part of humoral immune response. IgA is abundant in colostrum (mother's first milk) providing passive immunity to newborns.

nodes.label: Vaccination and Immunisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Based on 'memory' property of immune system. Vaccine = preparation of antigenic proteins of pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen introduced into body. Generates memory B and T-cells for rapid response on subsequent exposure. Passive immunisation uses preformed antibodies (e.g., tetanus antitoxin, snake antivenom). Recombinant DNA technology enables large-scale vaccine production (e.g., hepatitis B vaccine from yeast).

nodes.label: Active and Passive Immunity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Active immunity: host produces antibodies when exposed to antigens (living/dead microbes); slow but long-lasting. Includes natural infection and deliberate immunisation. Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies directly given to protect body; immediate but short-lived. Examples: colostrum (IgA) from mother, antibodies through placenta during pregnancy, antitoxin injections.

nodes.label: Lymphoid Organs
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organs where lymphocytes originate, mature, and proliferate. Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow (produces all blood cells including lymphocytes) and thymus (near heart, large at birth, shrinks by puberty, T-cell maturation). Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen (bean-shaped, filters blood, reservoir of erythrocytes), lymph nodes (trap antigens, activate lymphocytes), tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix. MALT constitutes about 50% of lymphoid tissue.

nodes.label: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Caused by HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), a retrovirus with RNA genome enclosed in envelope. First reported in 1981, killed 25+ million people. Transmission: sexual contact, contaminated blood transfusion, shared needles (IV drug users), infected mother to child via placenta. HIV enters macrophages, uses reverse transcriptase to form viral DNA which integrates into host DNA. Progressively destroys helper T-lymphocytes (T4 cells). Time lag of months to 5-10 years before symptoms. Diagnosed by ELISA test. No cure; anti-retroviral drugs only prolong life. NACO coordinates prevention in India.

nodes.label: Drugs and Alcohol Abuse
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Commonly abused drugs: (1) Opioids - heroin (diacetylmorphine, from Papaver somniferum latex via morphine acetylation), depressant; (2) Cannabinoids - from Cannabis sativa (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja), affect cardiovascular system; (3) Coca alkaloids - cocaine from Erythroxylum coca, stimulant, interferes with dopamine transport. Addiction leads to tolerance requiring higher doses. Adolescence (12-18 years) is most vulnerable period. Anabolic steroids misused in sports.

nodes.label: Tobacco and Smoking
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Tobacco contains nicotine (alkaloid) which stimulates adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking associated with cancers of lung, urinary bladder, throat, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease, gastric ulcer. Tobacco chewing increases risk of oral cavity cancer. Smoking increases CO in blood, reduces haemoglobin-bound oxygen causing oxygen deficiency.

nodes.label: Disease Prevention and Control
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Personal hygiene (clean body, clean food/water) and public hygiene (proper waste disposal, water reservoir cleaning) are essential. For air-borne diseases (pneumonia, cold): avoid close contact with infected persons. For vector-borne diseases (malaria, filariasis): eliminate stagnant water, use mosquito nets, introduce Gambusia fish (eat mosquito larvae), spray insecticides, use wire mesh on windows. Dengue and chikungunya transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.

nodes.label: Immune System
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Consists of lymphoid organs, tissues, cells, and soluble molecules (antibodies). Unique ability to recognize foreign antigens, respond to them, and remember them. Plays roles in allergic reactions, autoimmune diseases, and organ transplantation. Cell-mediated immunity responsible for graft rejection; tissue matching and blood group matching essential before transplants. Patients take immunosuppressants lifelong after transplants.

nodes.label: Animal Breeding
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Aims to increase yield and improve desirable qualities. Inbreeding: mating closely related individuals within same breed for 4-6 generations; increases homozygosity, exposes harmful recessive genes, accumulates superior genes; continued close inbreeding causes inbreeding depression (reduced fertility/productivity). Outbreeding includes out-crossing (same breed, no common ancestor for 4-6 gen), cross-breeding (different breeds, e.g., Hisardale sheep from Bikaneri ewes x Marino rams), and interspecific hybridisation (different species, e.g., mule).
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Artificial Insemination and MOET
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Artificial insemination: semen collected from selected male and injected into reproductive tract of selected female; can be frozen and transported. Overcomes problems of normal mating. MOET (Multiple Ovulation Embryo Transfer Technology): cow given FSH-like hormones to produce 6-8 eggs instead of one per cycle; mated with elite bull or artificially inseminated; fertilised eggs at 8-32 cell stage transferred to surrogate mothers. Used for cattle, sheep, rabbits, buffaloes, mares.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Apiculture (Bee-keeping)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Maintenance of hives of honeybees for honey production. Most common species: Apis indica. Honey has high nutritive value and medicinal use. Honeybees also produce beeswax (used in cosmetics, polishes). Bees are pollinators of crops like sunflower, Brassica, apple, and pear. Keeping beehives in crop fields during flowering increases pollination efficiency and improves both crop yield and honey yield. Not labour-intensive.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Fisheries
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Industry for catching, processing, and selling fish, shellfish, and aquatic animals (prawn, crab, lobster, edible oyster). Freshwater fishes: Catla, Rohu, Common carp. Marine fishes: Hilsa, Sardines, Mackerel, Pomfrets. Important for Indian economy, provides income to millions especially in coastal states. Aquaculture and pisciculture increase production of aquatic organisms. Blue Revolution implemented along lines of Green Revolution.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Plant Breeding
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Purposeful manipulation of plant species to create desired types with better yields and disease resistance. Five main steps: (1) Collection of variability (germplasm collection - all diverse alleles); (2) Evaluation and selection of parents; (3) Cross hybridisation of selected parents; (4) Selection and testing of superior recombinants (self-pollinated to homozygosity); (5) Testing, release and commercialisation (tested in farmers' fields for at least 3 seasons across agroclimatic zones). Classical breeding involves crossing pure lines followed by artificial selection.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Green Revolution
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Development of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice in mid-1960s through plant breeding techniques. Norman E. Borlaug (Nobel laureate) developed semi-dwarf wheat at International Centre for Wheat and Maize Improvement, Mexico. In India, M.S. Swaminathan collaborated with Borlaug. Wheat varieties Sonalika and Kalyan Sona introduced. Semi-dwarf rice from IR-8 (IRRI, Philippines) and Taichung Native-1 (Taiwan); derivatives Jaya and Ratna developed in India. Wheat: 11 to 75 million tonnes (1960-2000); Rice: 35 to 89.5 million tonnes.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Plant Breeding for Disease Resistance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Crop losses from fungal, bacterial, viral pathogens can reach 20-30% or total. Methods: conventional hybridisation and selection, mutation breeding. Key disease-resistant varieties: Himgiri wheat (leaf/stripe rust, hill bunt), Pusa Swarnim Brassica (white rust), Pusa Shubhra cauliflower (black rot, curl blight), Pusa Komal cowpea (bacterial blight), Pusa Sadabahar chilli (chilly mosaic, TMV, leaf curl). Mutation breeding: mung bean resistance to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew. Parbhani Kranti bhindi (yellow mosaic virus resistance from wild species).
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Plant Breeding for Insect Pest Resistance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Resistance may be morphological (hairy leaves resist jassids in cotton, solid stems resist stem sawfly in wheat), biochemical (high aspartic acid, low nitrogen/sugar resist maize stem borers), or physiological. Key varieties: Pusa Gaurav Brassica (aphids), Pusa Sem 2/3 flat bean (jassids, aphids, fruit borer), Pusa Sawani/A-4 okra (shoot/fruit borer). Smooth-leaved and nectarless cotton does not attract bollworms.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Tissue Culture
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Whole plants regenerated from explants (any plant part) grown in test tube under sterile conditions in special nutrient media. Based on totipotency - capacity of any cell to generate a whole plant. Medium requires carbon source (sucrose), inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators (auxins, cytokinins). Micropropagation: producing thousands of genetically identical plants (somaclones). Plants like tomato, banana, apple produced commercially. Virus-free plants obtained by culturing meristems (apical/axillary) which are virus-free even in infected plants.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Somatic Hybridisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Process of fusing isolated protoplasts from two different plant varieties, each with desirable characters, to get hybrid protoplasts which grow into new plants (somatic hybrids). Cell walls digested to isolate naked protoplasts (surrounded by plasma membranes). Pomato was created by fusing tomato and potato protoplasts, but lacked desired character combination for commercial use. Offers potential for creating novel plant varieties beyond sexual hybridisation limits.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Sugarcane Breeding
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Saccharum barberi originally grown in north India had poor sugar content and yield. Saccharum officinarum (tropical cane, south India) had thicker stems and higher sugar content but did not grow well in north India. The two species were successfully crossed to combine high yield, thick stems, high sugar content, and ability to grow in north Indian sugar cane areas. Example of interspecific hybridisation in plant breeding.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Mutation Breeding
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Creating genetic variations through changes in base sequences within genes using chemicals or radiations (gamma radiations). The mutant plants with desirable characters are selected for breeding. Used when conventional breeding has limited disease resistance genes. In mung bean, resistance to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew were induced by mutations. Also involves selection among somaclonal variants.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Amount of oxygen consumed if all organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. BOD test measures rate of oxygen uptake by microorganisms in water sample - indirect measure of organic matter present. Greater BOD = more polluting potential. Sewage treatment reduces BOD significantly. After BOD reduction, effluent passes to settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment as activated sludge. Part of activated sludge recycled to aeration tank as inoculum; rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters.

nodes.label: Activated Sludge Process
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In secondary sewage treatment, after BOD reduction, effluent passes to settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment as activated sludge. Small part pumped back to aeration tank as inoculum. Major part goes to anaerobic sludge digesters where anaerobic bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi, producing biogas (methane, hydrogen sulphide, CO2). Effluent from secondary treatment released into natural water bodies. Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan aim to build more STPs.

nodes.label: Methanogens
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce methane along with CO2 and H2. Common example: Methanobacterium. Found in anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and in rumen of cattle where they help break down cellulose. Cattle dung (gobar) is rich in methanogens, making it suitable for biogas production. Key organisms linking sewage treatment and biogas production.

nodes.label: Genetic Engineering
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Techniques to alter chemistry of genetic material (DNA/RNA), introduce into host organisms, and change phenotype of host. Overcomes limitations of traditional hybridisation (which includes undesirable genes along with desired ones). Allows isolation and introduction of only desired genes. Three basic steps: (1) identification of DNA with desirable genes; (2) introduction of identified DNA into host; (3) maintenance and transfer of introduced DNA to progeny.

nodes.label: Bioprocess Engineering
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Maintenance of sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes to enable growth of only desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities. Essential for manufacturing biotechnological products like antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes. One of two core techniques (along with genetic engineering) enabling modern biotechnology.

nodes.label: Restriction Enzymes (Restriction Endonucleases)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. First isolated in 1963 from E. coli. Hind II was the first characterised restriction endonuclease (recognises specific 6 base pair sequence). Over 900 restriction enzymes isolated from 230+ bacterial strains. Naming convention: first letter from genus, next two from species (e.g., EcoRI = Escherichia coli RY13, R from strain). Two types of nucleases: exonucleases (remove nucleotides from ends) and endonucleases (cut at specific internal positions).

nodes.label: Palindromic Sequences and Sticky Ends
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Restriction endonucleases recognise specific palindromic nucleotide sequences in DNA. A DNA palindrome reads the same on both strands in 5' to 3' direction (e.g., 5'-GAATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAAG-5' for EcoRI). Enzymes cut slightly away from centre of palindrome but between same two bases on opposite strands, leaving overhanging single-stranded portions called sticky ends. Sticky ends form hydrogen bonds with complementary cut counterparts, facilitating action of DNA ligase to join fragments.

nodes.label: Gel Electrophoresis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Technique to separate DNA fragments by size. DNA fragments are negatively charged, move towards anode under electric field through agarose gel matrix (natural polymer from seaweeds). Smaller fragments migrate farther (sieving effect). Separated DNA visualised by staining with ethidium bromide followed by UV radiation exposure (bright orange bands). Separated bands cut from gel and DNA extracted (elution). Purified fragments used for constructing recombinant DNA.

nodes.label: Cloning Vectors
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Plasmids and bacteriophages that replicate within bacterial cells independent of chromosomal DNA. Key features required: (1) Origin of replication (ori) - sequence where replication starts, controls copy number; (2) Selectable marker - genes for antibiotic resistance (ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, kanamycin) to identify transformants; (3) Cloning sites - preferably single recognition site for restriction enzymes. pBR322 is a widely used E. coli cloning vector with amp-R and tet-R genes.

nodes.label: pBR322 Vector
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Widely used E. coli cloning vector. Contains ampicillin resistance (amp-R) and tetracycline resistance (tet-R) genes as selectable markers. Has restriction sites for EcoRI, BamHI, SalI, PvuII, PstI, ClaI, HindIII. Foreign DNA inserted at BamHI site in tet-R gene causes insertional inactivation - recombinants grow on ampicillin but not tetracycline, while non-recombinants grow on both. 'rop' gene codes for proteins involved in plasmid replication.

nodes.label: Insertional Inactivation and Selection
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Method to distinguish recombinants from non-recombinants. When foreign DNA inserted into antibiotic resistance gene, it inactivates that gene. Alternative method: recombinant DNA inserted within coding sequence of beta-galactosidase enzyme gene. Non-recombinants produce blue colonies on chromogenic substrate; recombinants (with insert inactivating beta-galactosidase) produce colourless colonies. Blue-white screening is more efficient than dual antibiotic plate method.

nodes.label: Ti Plasmid (Agrobacterium)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Tumor inducing plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of dicot plants. Delivers T-DNA to transform normal plant cells into tumors that produce chemicals for pathogen. Modified into a cloning vector: no longer pathogenic but retains gene delivery mechanism for various plants. Similarly, disarmed retroviruses used as vectors for delivering genes into animal cells. Key vector for plant genetic engineering.

nodes.label: Competent Host Cells and Transformation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: DNA cannot pass through cell membranes (hydrophilic). Bacteria made competent by treating with divalent cation (calcium/CaCl2) to increase DNA uptake efficiency through cell wall pores. Heat shock method: cells incubated with recombinant DNA on ice, briefly at 42 degrees C, then back on ice. Other methods: micro-injection (directly into animal cell nucleus), biolistics/gene gun (high velocity gold/tungsten microparticles coated with DNA for plants), disarmed pathogen vectors.

nodes.label: Recombinant DNA Technology
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Construction of first recombinant DNA by Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer in 1972. Linked antibiotic resistance gene (cut from plasmid using restriction enzyme) with native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium using DNA ligase. Transferred to E. coli which replicated it using host DNA polymerase. Key process: cut source DNA and vector with same restriction enzyme, mix gene of interest with cut vector, add ligase to create recombinant DNA. Both vector and source DNA must be cut with same restriction enzyme.

nodes.label: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Technique to amplify gene/DNA of interest in vitro using two sets of primers (short synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to DNA regions) and DNA polymerase. Three steps per cycle: (1) Denaturation - high temperature separates double-stranded DNA; (2) Primer annealing - primers bind to complementary regions; (3) Extension - DNA polymerase extends primers using nucleotides. Uses thermostable Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus (remains active at high temperature). Can amplify DNA approximately 1 billion times (30 cycles). Amplified fragment can be ligated with vector for cloning.

nodes.label: DNA Isolation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: To cut DNA with restriction enzymes, it must be pure and free from other macromolecules. Cell opened using enzymes: lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plant cells), chitinase (fungus). RNA removed by ribonuclease; proteins removed by protease. Other molecules removed by appropriate treatments. Purified DNA precipitates out after addition of chilled ethanol, visible as fine threads in suspension that can be collected by spooling.

nodes.label: Bioreactors
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Vessels (100-1000 litres) for large-scale production where raw materials are biologically converted into specific products using microbial, plant, animal, or human cells. Provide optimal growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen). Most common type: stirred-tank bioreactor (cylindrical with curved base). Has agitator system, oxygen delivery system, foam control, temperature/pH control, and sampling ports. Sparged stirred-tank type uses sterile air bubbles.

nodes.label: Downstream Processing
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Series of processes after biosynthetic stage to prepare product for marketing. Includes separation and purification of the product. Product formulated with suitable preservatives. Undergoes thorough clinical trials (for drugs). Strict quality control testing required for each product. Varies from product to product. Essential final step in biotechnological product development.

nodes.label: DNA Ligase
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Enzyme that joins cut DNA molecules at their ends. Acts on sticky ends created by restriction enzymes cutting palindromic sequences. Essential for linking antibiotic resistance gene with plasmid vector to create recombinant DNA. When source DNA and vector DNA are cut with same restriction enzyme, the resulting fragments have compatible sticky ends that can be joined by DNA ligase.

nodes.label: Selectable Markers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Genes in vectors that help identify and eliminate non-transformants while selecting transformants. Commonly used: genes encoding resistance to antibiotics (ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, kanamycin). Normal E. coli cells lack antibiotic resistance. Transformed cells with recombinant DNA carrying resistance gene grow on antibiotic-containing medium while untransformed cells die. Alternative: chromogenic substrate-based selection (blue-white screening with beta-galactosidase).

nodes.label: Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Pioneers of recombinant DNA technology. In 1972, they constructed the first artificial recombinant DNA molecule. Boyer discovered restriction enzymes with useful properties (sticky ends) at UCSF. Cohen at Stanford studied plasmids in bacterial cells and developed methods to remove and reinsert them. Together, they combined DNA splicing with plasmid reinsertion to recombine DNA segments and insert them in bacterial cells, founding the discipline of biotechnology.

nodes.label: Recombinant Protein Production
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: When a protein-encoding gene is expressed in a heterologous host, the product is called recombinant protein. Cells with cloned genes of interest grown in laboratory, then scaled up. Continuous culture system: used medium drained from one side, fresh medium added from other to maintain cells in exponential/log phase for higher biomass and greater protein yields. Small volume cultures insufficient; bioreactors needed for large-scale production.

nodes.label: Genetically Engineered Insulin
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Insulin previously extracted from pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs, causing allergic reactions in some patients. Insulin has two short polypeptide chains (A and B) linked by disulphide bridges. Synthesised as pro-hormone with extra C peptide removed during maturation. In 1983, Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences for A and B chains, introduced in E. coli plasmids. Chains produced separately, extracted, combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin identical to natural molecule.

nodes.label: Gene Therapy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Collection of methods to correct gene defects diagnosed in child/embryo by inserting genes into person's cells and tissues. First clinical gene therapy in 1990: 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency (crucial enzyme for immune system, caused by gene deletion). Lymphocytes grown in culture, functional ADA cDNA introduced using retroviral vector, cells returned to patient. Not permanent - requires periodic infusion. If gene introduced into bone marrow cells at early embryonic stage, could be permanent cure. ADA deficiency also treated by bone marrow transplant or enzyme replacement therapy.

nodes.label: ADA (Adenosine Deaminase) Deficiency
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Genetic disorder caused by deletion of gene for adenosine deaminase enzyme, crucial for immune system function. First disease treated with gene therapy (1990). Can be treated by: (1) bone marrow transplantation; (2) enzyme replacement therapy (injecting functional ADA); (3) gene therapy - introducing functional ADA cDNA via retroviral vector into patient's lymphocytes. Treatments (1) and (2) not completely curative. Permanent cure possible if gene introduced at early embryonic stage.

nodes.label: Molecular Diagnostics
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Techniques for early disease diagnosis using recombinant DNA technology. PCR detects very low concentrations of pathogens by amplifying their nucleic acid before symptoms appear. Routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and mutations in cancer patients. DNA/RNA probe (tagged with radioactive molecule) hybridised to complementary DNA in cell clone, detected by autoradiography; mutated gene won't appear on film. ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay): based on antigen-antibody interaction, detects pathogen antigens or antibodies against pathogen.

nodes.label: ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Diagnostic technique based on principle of antigen-antibody interaction. Detects infection by pathogen through presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins) or by detecting antibodies synthesised against the pathogen. Widely used diagnostic test for AIDS. Also used in detecting various other infections. Key molecular diagnostic tool alongside PCR.

nodes.label: Population Attributes
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Populations possess attributes individuals do not: birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio, age distribution. Birth rate = per capita births (e.g., 8 new plants from 20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year). Age pyramid shapes: expanding (growing population), stable, and declining. Population density (N) measured by total number, biomass, or percent cover. Tiger census uses indirect methods like pug marks and fecal pellets.

nodes.label: Exponential Growth (J-curve)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: When resources are unlimited, population grows exponentially following dN/dt = rN, where r is intrinsic rate of natural increase (b-d). Integral form: Nt = N0 * e^(rt). Produces a J-shaped curve. Example r values: Norway rat = 0.015, flour beetle = 0.12, India human population (1981) = 0.0205. Even slow-growing organisms like elephants can reach enormous numbers without checks. Named after the chess-and-wheat-grain analogy of exponential doubling.

nodes.label: Logistic Growth (S-curve)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: When resources are limited, population growth follows Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth: dN/dt = rN[(K-N)/K], where K is carrying capacity. Produces a sigmoid S-shaped curve with lag phase, acceleration, deceleration, and asymptote at K. More realistic than exponential model for most natural populations. As N approaches K, (K-N)/K approaches zero, slowing growth. The fittest individuals survive competition for limited resources.

nodes.label: Carrying Capacity (K)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The maximum population size a habitat can sustain with its available resources. Denoted as K in the logistic growth equation. When population density N equals K, growth rate becomes zero. Population density fluctuates around K due to changes in natality, mortality, immigration, and emigration. The equation Nt+1 = Nt + [(B+I) - (D+E)] governs population density changes.

nodes.label: Life History Variation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisms evolve reproductive strategies to maximise Darwinian fitness (high r value). Some breed once in lifetime (semelparous) like Pacific salmon and bamboo. Others breed many times (iteroparous) like most birds and mammals. Some produce many small offspring (r-selected: oysters, pelagic fishes) while others produce few large offspring (K-selected: birds, mammals). Life history traits evolve in response to habitat constraints.

nodes.label: Competition
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Interaction where both species suffer (-, -). Occurs between related or unrelated species competing for same resources (e.g., flamingoes and fishes competing for zooplankton in South American lakes). Interference competition reduces feeding efficiency even when resources are abundant. Connell's barnacle experiments on Scottish rocky coasts: larger Balanus excludes smaller Chathamalus from intertidal zone. Competitive release: restricted species expands range when competitor is removed.

nodes.label: Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: States that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely; the competitively inferior one will be eliminated. Example: Abingdon tortoise in Galapagos became extinct after goat introduction. However, species can co-exist through resource partitioning: MacArthur showed five warbler species on the same tree avoided competition through different foraging patterns and timings.

nodes.label: Mutualism
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Interaction where both species benefit (+, +). Lichens: mutualism between fungus and algae/cyanobacteria. Mycorrhizae: fungi help plant absorb nutrients, plant provides carbohydrates. Fig-wasp mutualism: each fig species has a specific partner wasp for pollination; wasp uses fruit for oviposition and larval nutrition. Ophrys orchid uses sexual deceit - petal resembles female bee, male bee 'pseudocopulates' and transfers pollen. Co-evolution is tightly linked in plant-pollinator mutualisms.

nodes.label: Air Pollution and Control
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Air pollutants from thermal power plants, smelters, industries, and automobiles cause injury to all living organisms. Particulate and gaseous pollutants must be filtered before release. PM 2.5 (2.5 micrometers or less, per CPCB) causes greatest harm to human health: inhaled deep into lungs, causes respiratory symptoms, inflammation, premature death. Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, amended 1987 to include noise as air pollutant. Noise >150 dB (jet takeoff) can permanently damage ear drums.

nodes.label: Electrostatic Precipitator
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Removes over 99% of particulate matter from thermal power plant exhaust. Mechanism: electrode wires maintained at several thousand volts produce a corona releasing electrons. Electrons attach to dust particles giving them net negative charge. Grounded collecting plates attract the charged particles. Air velocity between plates must be low enough for dust to fall. Cannot remove very fine particulates (PM 2.5). Most widely used particulate removal device.

nodes.label: Scrubber
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Removes gaseous pollutants like sulphur dioxide from industrial exhaust. Mechanism: exhaust is passed through a spray of water or lime which absorbs the gases. Works alongside electrostatic precipitators which handle particulate matter. Together these technologies form the primary air pollution control systems for industrial smokestacks.

nodes.label: Water Pollution and Control
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Domestic sewage: mere 0.1% impurities make water unfit for use. Contains suspended solids, colloidal material (fecal matter, bacteria), dissolved materials (nitrates, phosphates, toxic metals). Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 safeguards water resources. Industrial waste contains heavy metals (mercury, cadmium, copper, lead - density >5 g/cm3) and organic compounds. Thermal wastewater from power plants harms temperature-sensitive aquatic organisms.

nodes.label: Algal Bloom
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Excessive growth of planktonic (free-floating) algae caused by large amounts of nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) in water bodies. Imparts distinct colour to water. Causes deterioration of water quality and fish mortality. Some bloom-forming algae are extremely toxic to humans and animals. Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), called 'Terror of Bengal', grows abundantly in eutrophic waters and disrupts ecosystem dynamics. Related to eutrophication process.

nodes.label: Biomagnification (Biological Magnification)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Increase in concentration of a toxicant at successive trophic levels in an aquatic food chain. Occurs because toxic substance accumulated by an organism cannot be metabolised or excreted and is passed to next trophic level. Well-known for mercury and DDT. DDT concentration: 0.003 ppb in water -> 0.04 ppm in zooplankton -> 0.5 ppm in small fish -> 2 ppm in large fish -> 25 ppm in fish-eating birds. High DDT concentrations disturb calcium metabolism in birds, causing eggshell thinning, premature breaking, and population decline.

nodes.label: Eutrophication
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Natural aging of a lake by nutrient enrichment. Natural process spans thousands of years: young lake (cold, clear, little life) -> nutrient accumulation from streams -> increased fertility -> organic deposits on bottom -> lake grows shallower and warmer -> marsh plants fill in basin -> bog -> land conversion. Cultural/Accelerated Eutrophication: drastically sped up by human pollutants (sewage, agricultural/industrial waste). Prime contaminants: nitrates and phosphates stimulate algal growth, deplete dissolved oxygen, leading to fish kills. Lake can literally 'choke to death'.

nodes.label: Solid Waste Management
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Municipal solid wastes: paper, food wastes, plastics, glass, metals, rubber, leather, textile from homes, offices, hospitals. Open dumps breed rats and flies. Sanitary landfills: wastes compacted in depression/trench, covered with dirt daily; risk of chemical seepage into groundwater. Three waste categories: biodegradable, recyclable, non-biodegradable. Hospital wastes (hazardous, with pathogens) require incineration. E-wastes (defunct electronics): exported from developed to developing countries; recycling recovers copper, iron, silicon, nickel, gold but exposes workers to toxics.

nodes.label: Integrated Organic Farming
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Cyclical, zero-waste procedure where waste products from one process become nutrients for another. Case study: Ramesh Chandra Dagar in Sonipat, Haryana integrates bee-keeping, dairy management, water harvesting, composting, and agriculture in a self-supporting chain. No chemical fertilisers needed: cattle dung used as manure, crop waste for compost/natural gas. Founded Haryana Kisan Welfare Club with 5,000 farmer members. Contrasts with Green Revolution approach of inorganic fertilisers and pesticides.

nodes.label: Radioactive Waste
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Nuclear energy problems: accidental leakage (Three Mile Island, Chernobyl) and safe disposal of radioactive waste. Nuclear radiation causes mutations at very high rate; high doses are lethal, lower doses cause cancer and other disorders. Recommended disposal: pre-treated waste in shielded containers buried ~500 m deep in rocks. Faces public opposition. Nuclear waste is an extremely potent pollutant requiring utmost caution.

nodes.label: Montreal Protocol
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: International treaty signed at Montreal, Canada in 1987 (effective 1989) to control emission of ozone depleting substances (ODS). Laid down separate roadmaps for developed and developing countries for reducing CFC and other ODS emissions. One of the most successful international environmental agreements. Subsequent protocols have set further targets. Recognises the deleterious effects of ozone depletion on living organisms.

nodes.label: Deforestation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Conversion of forested areas to non-forested ones. ~40% of tropical forests lost vs only 1% in temperate regions. India: forest cover shrunk from 30% (early 20th century) to 21.54% (end of century); National Forest Policy 1988 recommends 33% for plains and 67% for hills. Causes: agricultural conversion, timber, firewood, cattle ranching. Slash and burn agriculture (Jhum cultivation in NE India): farmers cut/burn trees, use ash as fertiliser, cultivate, then move on. Consequences: increased atmospheric CO2, biodiversity loss, hydrologic cycle disruption, soil erosion, desertification.

nodes.label: Reforestation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The restocking of destroyed forests by planting new trees, preferably of the same species that were found in the original forest. Can occur naturally if deforested areas are left undisturbed. Essential for retaining green wealth and combating the effects of deforestation.

nodes.label: Joint Forest Management (JFM)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Concept introduced by Government of India in 1980s to work closely with local communities for protecting and managing forests. Communities provide services to the forest and in return get benefits of various forest products (fruits, gum, rubber, medicine). Enables sustainable forest conservation through people's participation. Based on recognition that local community involvement is crucial for effective conservation.

nodes.label: Arcata Marsh Integrated Wastewater Treatment
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Town of Arcata, northern California coast, created integrated wastewater treatment using natural systems. Two-stage cleaning: (a) conventional sedimentation, filtering, and chlorine treatment; (b) innovative series of six connected marshes over 60 hectares with appropriate plants, algae, fungi, and bacteria that neutralise, absorb, and assimilate pollutants. Water purified naturally as it flows through marshes. Marshes also became biodiversity sanctuary. Maintained by citizens group FOAM (Friends of the Arcata Marsh). Also notable: EcoSan dry composting toilets in Kerala and Sri Lanka recycle excreta as natural fertiliser.

nodes.label: Sources of Food
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The main sources of food for humans are plants and animals. Plants provide grains, cereals, vegetables, and fruits, while animals provide milk, meat, and eggs. There is wide regional variation in the food eaten across India.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Edible Plant Parts
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Different parts of plants are eaten as food -- roots (carrot, radish), stems (potato, ginger), leaves (spinach, cabbage), flowers (broccoli, pumpkin flowers), fruits (mango, apple), and seeds (wheat, rice, mustard). Some plants like mustard have multiple edible parts.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Herbivore
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals that eat only plants or plant products are called herbivores. Examples include cow, buffalo, deer, and goat. They have specialized teeth and digestive systems adapted for processing plant matter.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Carnivore
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals that eat only other animals are called carnivores. Examples include lion, tiger, and spider. They are predators with adaptations like sharp teeth and claws for hunting and consuming flesh.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Omnivore
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals that eat both plants and animals are called omnivores. Examples include dog, crow, bear, and human beings. This dietary flexibility allows omnivores to survive in varied environments.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Food Ingredients
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Every food item is made from one or more raw materials called ingredients. These ingredients are obtained from plants or animals. For example, dal is made from pulses (plant), while paneer comes from milk (animal).
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Animal Products as Food
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals provide several food products. Cows, goats, and buffaloes give milk, which is used to make butter, cream, cheese, and curd. Hens provide eggs. Fish, chicken, and goat meat are common animal-based food items.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Nectar and Honey
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Bees collect nectar (sweet juices) from flowers and convert it into honey, storing it in their beehives. Honey is a food source that comes from neither plants nor animals directly, but is produced by bees from plant nectar.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Sprouted Seeds
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: When dry seeds like moong or chana are soaked in water and kept moist, they germinate and produce sprouts. Sprouted seeds are nutritious and can be eaten raw or boiled. Sprouting increases the nutritional value of seeds.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Food Variety in India
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: There is great variation in the food eaten in different regions of India, reflecting diverse agricultural practices, climatic conditions, and cultural preferences. Despite this variety, all meals draw from plants and animals as primary sources.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Food Security (Basic)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Many people in India do not get sufficient food. There is a need to find ways to produce more food and ensure its equitable distribution so that it is easily available to each person in the country.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Food Chain (Basic)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Plants produce food through photosynthesis. Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat herbivores, and omnivores eat both. This chain of eating relationships forms the basis of the food chain in any ecosystem.
nodes.chapter_title: Food: Where Does It Come From?

nodes.label: Cotton
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A plant fibre obtained from cotton bolls (fruits of the cotton plant). Grown in regions with black soil and warm climate. Major cotton-growing states in India include Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Andhra Pradesh. Seeds are separated by ginning.

nodes.label: Jute
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A plant fibre obtained from the stem of the jute plant. Cultivated during the rainy season mainly in West Bengal, Bihar, and Assam. Harvested at flowering stage; stems are immersed in water to rot, then fibres are separated by hand (retting).

nodes.label: Ginning
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process of separating cotton fibres from their seeds. Traditionally done by hand, now also done by machines. An essential step in cotton processing before fibres can be spun into yarn.

nodes.label: Spinning
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process of making yarn from fibres by drawing out and twisting them together. Done using hand spindle (takli), charkha, or spinning machines. Charkha was popularised by Mahatma Gandhi during the Independence movement.

nodes.label: Weaving
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process of arranging two sets of yarns together to make fabric. Done on looms which can be hand-operated (handloom) or power-operated (powerloom). India has a long tradition of handloom weaving.

nodes.label: Knitting
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A process of making fabric using a single yarn, unlike weaving which uses two sets. Used for making sweaters, socks, and many clothing items. Can be done by hand or on machines.

nodes.label: Khadi
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Cloth made from homespun yarn, promoted by Mahatma Gandhi during the Independence movement. Gandhi encouraged people to wear khadi and shun imported British cloth. The Khadi and Village Industries Commission was established in 1956 to promote it.

nodes.label: History of Clothing
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ancient people used bark, leaves, animal skins, and furs. Early Indians wore cotton fabrics from the Ganga region. Ancient Egyptians used cotton and flax near the river Nile. Stitching came later with the invention of the sewing needle; earlier fabrics were draped.

nodes.label: Flax
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A plant that gives natural fibres, used in ancient times along with cotton. Cultivated near the river Nile in ancient Egypt for making fabrics. One of the earliest fibres used by humans for clothing.

nodes.label: Acid Rain
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Rain containing acids formed when pollutant gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rainwater. Acid rain damages buildings (especially marble like Taj Mahal), kills aquatic life, and harms vegetation. It is a major environmental concern.

nodes.label: Soil Erosion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The removal of the top layer of soil by wind, water, or human activities. Deforestation, overgrazing, and improper farming accelerate erosion. It leads to loss of fertile topsoil. Prevention includes afforestation, terrace farming, and contour ploughing.

nodes.label: Soil Pollution
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Contamination of soil by excessive use of pesticides, fertilisers, industrial waste, and non-biodegradable materials like polythene. Soil pollution reduces soil fertility, affects crop quality, and can contaminate groundwater.

nodes.label: Water Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The continuous circulation of water in nature through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff. Water evaporates from oceans and land, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back to oceans through rivers. Also called the hydrological cycle.

nodes.label: Groundwater
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Water found below the Earth's surface in soil and rock crevices. It is the source for wells, tubewells, and handpumps. Groundwater is recharged by rainwater seeping through soil. Over-extraction has led to declining water tables in many parts of India.

nodes.label: Water Table
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The upper level of groundwater below the Earth's surface. The water table varies with rainfall, extraction, and season. In many Indian cities, the water table has dropped significantly due to over-extraction and reduced groundwater recharge from urbanisation.

nodes.label: Groundwater Depletion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The decline in groundwater levels caused by excessive pumping, reduced recharge due to concrete surfaces, and deforestation. Increases with growing population and agriculture. Can lead to wells drying up and land subsidence. A critical environmental issue in India.

nodes.label: Rainwater Harvesting
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The collection and storage of rainwater for later use. Rooftop harvesting collects rain from roofs into tanks or underground reservoirs. It recharges groundwater and reduces dependence on other water sources. Mandated by law in several Indian states.

nodes.label: Aquifer
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Underground layers of porous rock, sand, or gravel that store and transmit groundwater. Aquifers are the primary source of groundwater for wells and borewells. Their recharge depends on rainfall and soil permeability. Major aquifers in India include the Gangetic alluvial aquifer.

nodes.label: Traditional Water Harvesting (Bawri)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Traditional structures in India for collecting and storing rainwater. Bawris (stepwells) in Rajasthan, johads, tanks, and check dams were used historically. These ancient systems are being revived as modern solutions to water scarcity.

nodes.label: Contaminants in Sewage
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Sewage contains organic impurities (human faeces, food waste), inorganic impurities (chemicals, pesticides, heavy metals), nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus causing eutrophication), bacteria, and viruses. Each type requires specific treatment methods.

nodes.label: Natural Gas
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An important fossil fuel that is easy to transport through pipes. Stored under high pressure as CNG (Compressed Natural Gas), used for power generation and as a cleaner transport fuel. In India, found in Tripura, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, and Krishna Godavari delta. Also used for manufacturing chemicals and fertilisers.

nodes.label: CNG (Compressed Natural Gas)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Natural gas stored under high pressure, used as a cleaner fuel for transport vehicles because it produces harmful products in very small amounts. Can be supplied directly through pipelines to homes and factories. Networks exist in Vadodara, parts of Delhi, and other places in India.

nodes.label: Combustion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A chemical process in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give off heat, and sometimes light. Requires three essentials: fuel, air (oxygen), and heat to reach ignition temperature. Fire can be controlled by removing any one of these requirements.

nodes.label: Ignition Temperature
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The lowest temperature at which a combustible substance catches fire. Different substances have different ignition temperatures. Kerosene oil has a lower ignition temperature than wood. Substances with very low ignition temperature are called inflammable substances.

nodes.label: Inflammable Substances
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Substances with very low ignition temperature that can easily catch fire with a flame. Examples include petrol, alcohol, and LPG. These require special care in storage and handling due to their high fire risk.

nodes.label: Rapid Combustion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Combustion where a gas or substance burns rapidly producing heat and light, such as when LPG burns on a gas stove. This is the most common controlled form of combustion used in homes and industry.

nodes.label: Spontaneous Combustion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Combustion where a material suddenly bursts into flames without any apparent external cause. Phosphorus burns in air at room temperature. Spontaneous combustion of coal dust has caused many disastrous fires in coal mines, and forest fires can occur due to sun's heat or lightning.

nodes.label: Flame Structure
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A flame has three zones: the innermost dark zone of unburnt vapours, the middle luminous zone of partial combustion (yellow, deposits carbon), and the outermost non-luminous zone of complete combustion (blue, hottest). Goldsmiths use the outermost zone to melt gold and silver.

nodes.label: Carbon Monoxide
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A very poisonous gas produced by incomplete combustion of carbon fuels like coal and wood. Burning coal in a closed room can produce enough carbon monoxide to kill sleeping persons. It is colourless and odourless, making it especially dangerous.

nodes.label: Fire Extinguisher
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Devices that cut off oxygen supply or bring down fuel temperature. Water is common but unsuitable for electrical fires and oil fires. CO2 is the best extinguisher for electrical and inflammable material fires as it is heavier than oxygen and forms a blanket, also cooling the fuel.

nodes.label: Fuel
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A combustible substance used for producing heat energy. Can be solid (coal, wood), liquid (kerosene, petrol), or gaseous (natural gas, LPG). An ideal fuel is readily available, cheap, burns easily, produces large heat, and does not leave undesirable residues or pollute the environment.

nodes.label: Carbon Dioxide and Pollution
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Increased CO2 from burning fossil fuels is linked to global warming. Unburnt carbon particles from wood and coal cause respiratory diseases like asthma. CNG has replaced petrol and diesel in many vehicles because it produces harmful products in much smaller amounts.

nodes.label: Biosphere Reserve
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Large areas of protected land for conservation of wildlife, plant and animal resources, and traditional life of tribals. They help maintain biodiversity and culture. Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve contains Satpura National Park and Bori and Pachmarhi Wildlife Sanctuaries.

nodes.label: Wildlife Sanctuary
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Areas where animals are protected from any disturbance to them and their habitat. Unlike national parks, people living in sanctuaries are allowed limited activities like grazing livestock and collecting medicinal plants and firewood. Killing or capturing animals is strictly prohibited.

nodes.label: Endemic Species
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Species of plants and animals found exclusively in a particular area and not naturally found anywhere else. Sal and wild mango are endemic flora, and bison, Indian giant squirrel, and flying squirrel are endemic fauna of Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve. Destruction of habitat threatens their existence.

nodes.label: Endangered Species
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals whose numbers are diminishing to a level where they might face extinction. Examples include black buck, white eyed buck, elephant, golden cat, pink headed duck, gharial, marsh crocodile, python, rhinoceros, and tiger. Small animals are often at greater risk than larger ones.

nodes.label: Red Data Book
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An international source book that keeps a record of all endangered animals and plants. Maintained by an international organisation (IUCN). India also maintains its own Red Data Book for plants and animals found in India, tracking species at risk of extinction.

nodes.label: Species
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A group of populations capable of interbreeding, meaning members can reproduce fertile offspring only with members of their own species. Members of a species share common characteristics. This is the fundamental unit of biological classification.

nodes.label: Matter
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Anything that occupies space and has mass. Everything in the universe is made of matter. Early Indian philosophers classified matter as five elements: Panch Tatva (air, earth, fire, sky, water). Modern science classifies matter based on physical properties and chemical nature.

nodes.label: States of Matter
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Matter exists in three primary states: solid, liquid, and gas, determined by the arrangement and movement of particles. A fourth state, plasma, exists at very high temperatures (ionised gases in stars and neon signs). A fifth state, Bose-Einstein Condensate, exists at very low temperatures.

nodes.label: Solid
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A state of matter with definite shape and volume. Particles are closely packed with strong forces of attraction, vibrating about fixed positions. Solids are rigid and incompressible, maintaining shape even when force is applied. They have negligible compressibility.

nodes.label: Liquid
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A state of matter with definite volume but no definite shape, taking the shape of its container. Particles are less closely packed than solids with moderate forces of attraction. Liquids flow and can be poured. They are slightly compressible.

nodes.label: Gas
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A state of matter with neither definite shape nor volume, filling the entire container. Particles are far apart with very weak forces of attraction and move freely at high speeds. Gases are highly compressible, which is why LPG and CNG can be stored under pressure.

nodes.label: Boiling Point
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The temperature at which a liquid starts boiling and changes to gas throughout the bulk of the liquid. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure. Boiling point changes with pressure, which is why pressure cookers cook food faster.

nodes.label: Melting Point
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius. During melting, temperature remains constant despite continuous heating because heat energy is used to change the state rather than raise temperature (latent heat of fusion).

nodes.label: Latent Heat
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The heat energy absorbed or released during a change of state without any change in temperature. Latent heat of fusion is 334 kJ/kg for ice. Latent heat of vaporisation is 2260 kJ/kg for water. This energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles.

nodes.label: Sublimation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The direct change of a solid into vapour (gas) without passing through the liquid state. Examples include camphor, naphthalene balls, ammonium chloride, and dry ice (solid CO2). The reverse process is deposition.

nodes.label: Diffusion
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The inter-mixing of particles of two different types of matter on their own, due to random movement. Diffusion is fastest in gases and slowest in solids. It explains how smell of perfume reaches across a room and how aquatic animals use dissolved oxygen in water.

nodes.label: Plasma
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The fourth state of matter consisting of super-energised ionised particles. Found in stars where extremely high temperatures break atoms into charged particles. Fluorescent tubes and neon sign bulbs contain plasma created by electrical energy.

nodes.label: Biological Classification
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The systematic grouping of organisms based on shared characteristics. Developed by Carolus Linnaeus, the hierarchy runs: Kingdom, Phylum (Division for plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Whittaker's Five Kingdom classification is the most widely accepted modern system.

nodes.label: Five Kingdom Classification
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Proposed by R.H. Whittaker in 1969, organisms are classified into Monera (prokaryotic), Protista (unicellular eukaryotes), Fungi (heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin), Plantae (multicellular, autotrophic), and Animalia (multicellular, heterotrophic, no cell walls). Based on cell structure, mode of nutrition, and body organisation.

nodes.label: Kingdom Monera
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Prokaryotic organisms without a defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Includes bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae). Some are autotrophic, some heterotrophic. Cell wall may or may not be present. Includes nitrogen-fixing bacteria and disease-causing pathogens.

nodes.label: Kingdom Protista
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Unicellular eukaryotic organisms that use cilia, flagella, or pseudopodia for movement. Includes unicellular algae, diatoms, and protozoans. Some are autotrophic (like Euglena), others heterotrophic. Amoeba, Paramecium, and Plasmodium (malaria parasite) belong here.

nodes.label: Kingdom Fungi
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin. They are saprophytic (feeding on decaying matter) or parasitic. Body is made of thread-like hyphae forming a mycelium. Some have symbiotic relationships (lichens with algae, mycorrhiza with plants). Examples: yeast, mushroom, bread mould.

nodes.label: Kingdom Plantae
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Multicellular eukaryotic autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose. Use chlorophyll for photosynthesis. Classified into Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta (cryptogams, no seeds), Gymnosperms (naked seeds), and Angiosperms (covered seeds, flowering plants).

nodes.label: Kingdom Animalia
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Multicellular eukaryotic heterotrophs without cell walls. Most are mobile. Classified based on body design differentiation: Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Protochordata, and Vertebrata.

nodes.label: Phylum Arthropoda
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Probably the largest group of animals. Bilaterally symmetrical, segmented, with jointed legs and open circulatory system. Includes prawns, butterflies, houseflies, spiders, scorpions, crabs, and cockroaches. The name means jointed legs. Exoskeleton made of chitin.

nodes.label: Vertebrata
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals with a true vertebral column (backbone) and internal skeleton. Classified into Pisces (fish), Amphibia (dual life), Reptilia (crawling), Aves (birds), and Mammalia (milk-producing). All have bilateral symmetry, triploblastic body, and well-developed organ systems.

nodes.label: Class Pisces (Fish)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Aquatic vertebrates with streamlined body, scales, gills for breathing, and fins for swimming. Cold-blooded (poikilothermic). Skeleton may be cartilaginous (sharks, rays) or bony (tuna, rohu). Two-chambered heart. Lay eggs (oviparous).

nodes.label: Class Amphibia
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Vertebrates that live both in water and on land (dual life). Lack scales, have mucus-covered moist skin. Breathe through gills (as tadpoles) and lungs/skin (as adults). Three-chambered heart. Cold-blooded and oviparous. Examples: frogs, toads, salamanders.

nodes.label: Class Reptilia
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Cold-blooded vertebrates with dry, scaly skin, breathing through lungs. Three-chambered heart (crocodiles have four). Mostly oviparous with tough-shelled eggs. Examples: lizards, snakes, turtles, crocodiles. Adapted to terrestrial life, some are aquatic (marine turtles).

nodes.label: Class Aves (Birds)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Warm-blooded (homeothermic) vertebrates with feathers, hollow bones for flight, beaks, and forelimbs modified into wings. Four-chambered heart for efficient oxygenation. Lay hard-shelled eggs. Most can fly (except ostrich, penguin). Streamlined body shape aids flight.

nodes.label: Class Mammalia
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Warm-blooded vertebrates with mammary glands for milk production, hair/fur on skin, and four-chambered heart. Most are viviparous (except platypus and echidna which lay eggs). External ears (pinnae) present. Includes humans, whales, bats, elephants. Most advanced group of animals.

nodes.label: Binomial Nomenclature
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The system of naming organisms using two Latin words introduced by Carolus Linnaeus. The first word is the genus name (capitalised) and the second is the species name (lowercase). Written in italics when printed or underlined when handwritten. Example: Homo sapiens for humans.

nodes.label: Gymnosperms
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Plants bearing naked seeds not enclosed in a fruit. Usually perennial, evergreen, and woody. Examples include pines, deodar, and cycas. They have well-differentiated plant body with root, stem, and leaves but lack flowers and fruits.

nodes.label: Angiosperms
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Flowering plants bearing seeds enclosed within a fruit. Divided into monocots (one cotyledon, parallel veins: wheat, rice, maize) and dicots (two cotyledons, reticulate veins: pea, gram). Most diverse group of plants, forming the dominant land vegetation.

nodes.label: Inflammation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The body's initial response to infection, characterised by swelling, redness, heat, and pain at the site of infection. Triggered by the immune system recruiting cells to the affected area. An active immune system causes fever as a side effect of fighting infection.

nodes.label: Biosphere
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The life-supporting zone of the Earth where the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere interact, making life possible. Unique to Earth among known planets. Life exists from deep ocean floors to high mountains. The biosphere contains all ecosystems and biodiversity.

nodes.label: Atmosphere
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The blanket of air surrounding the Earth, composed of 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and small amounts of CO2, water vapour, and other gases. Keeps Earth's temperature moderate through the greenhouse effect. Protects against UV radiation. Wind patterns are caused by uneven heating of air.

nodes.label: Greenhouse Effect
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Some atmospheric gases (CO2, methane, water vapour) trap heat reflected by Earth's surface, preventing its escape to space, similar to glass in a greenhouse. Essential for maintaining Earth's temperature, but increased CO2 from fossil fuels causes enhanced greenhouse effect leading to global warming.

nodes.label: Soil Formation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Soil is formed by weathering of rocks by physical (sun heating, water freezing), chemical (dissolution), and biological (lichens, plant roots) factors over millions of years. Soil contains mineral particles, humus (decayed organic matter), water, air, and living organisms. Essential for terrestrial life.

nodes.label: Rainfall and Wind Patterns
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Caused by uneven heating of air over land and water bodies, creating winds. Water evaporates, rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds. Rainfall patterns depend on prevailing winds and topography. Monsoon patterns in India are driven by differential heating of land and Indian Ocean.
